sentences.text: Two retirees with the same balance, the same withdrawals and the same average return.
sentences.spoken: Two retirees with the same balance, the same withdrawals and the same average return.

sentences.text: One ran out of money in 1991.
sentences.spoken: One ran out of money in nineteen ninety-one.

sentences.text: So what decided it?
sentences.spoken: So what decided it?

sentences.text: It is January 1966.
sentences.spoken: It is January nineteen sixty-six.

sentences.text: The first retiree starts with $1 million, measured in 1966 dollars.
sentences.spoken: The first retiree starts with one million dollars, measured in nineteen sixty-six dollars.

sentences.text: They retire at the start of a hard decade for markets, though nobody knows it yet.
sentences.spoken: They retire at the start of a hard decade for markets... though nobody knows it yet.

sentences.text: By the end of this video, you will know which ten years decided the fate of this retiree, and whether the same thing held for every start year since 1928.
sentences.spoken: By the end of this video, you will know which ten years decided the fate of this retiree... and whether the same thing held, for every start year since nineteen twenty-eight.

sentences.text: The money sits in a portfolio of 60% stocks and 40% bonds.
sentences.spoken: The money sits in a portfolio of sixty percent stocks and forty percent bonds.

sentences.text: The stocks are the Standard & Poor's 500 index, with dividends reinvested.
sentences.spoken: The stocks are the Standard & Poor's five hundred index, with dividends reinvested.

sentences.text: The bonds are 10-year US Treasury bonds.
sentences.spoken: The bonds are ten-year U.S. Treasury bonds.

sentences.text: Every January, the portfolio is rebalanced back to that mix.
sentences.spoken: Every January, the portfolio is rebalanced back to that mix.

sentences.text: In the first year, the retiree withdraws 4% of the starting balance.
sentences.spoken: In the first year, the retiree withdraws four percent of the starting balance.

sentences.text: That is $40,000, in 1966 dollars.
sentences.spoken: That is forty thousand dollars, in nineteen sixty-six dollars.

sentences.text: After that, the withdrawal rises each year with the previous year's inflation, so it always buys the same groceries.
sentences.spoken: After that, the withdrawal rises each year with the previous year's inflation, so it always buys the same groceries.

sentences.text: In real terms, it never changes.
sentences.spoken: In real terms, it never changes.

sentences.text: In nominal terms, the dollars of the day, it climbs every year.
sentences.spoken: In nominal terms, the dollars of the day, it climbs every year.

sentences.text: The plan runs for 30 years, from 1966 through 1995.
sentences.spoken: The plan runs for thirty years, from nineteen sixty-six through nineteen ninety-five.

sentences.text: No taxes, no fees.
sentences.spoken: No taxes, no fees.

sentences.text: We keep the model this bare on purpose, so that one thing can change at a time.
sentences.spoken: We keep the model this bare on purpose, so that one thing can change at a time.

sentences.text: The data is US only, and this is history, not a forecast.
sentences.spoken: The data is U.S. only, and this is history, not a forecast.

sentences.text: Now meet the second retiree.
sentences.spoken: Now meet the second retiree.

sentences.text: The mirror retiree lives through the exact same 30 annual returns, but in reverse order.
sentences.spoken: The mirror retiree lives through the exact same thirty annual returns, but in reverse order.

sentences.text: The return of 1995 arrives first, and the return of 1966 arrives last.
sentences.spoken: The return of nineteen ninety-five arrives first, and the return of nineteen sixty-six arrives last.

sentences.text: This retiree is illustrative: no one lived through these years in this order.
sentences.spoken: This retiree is illustrative: no one lived through these years in this order.

sentences.text: Inflation stays in its real calendar order, so both retirees take out the same dollars every year.
sentences.spoken: Inflation stays in its real calendar order, so both retirees take out the same dollars every year.

sentences.text: Here is the question this first part answers.
sentences.spoken: Here is the question... this first part answers.

sentences.text: If two people earn the same average return, do they end up in the same place?
sentences.spoken: If two people earn the same average return... do they end up, in the same place?

sentences.text: The portfolio of the 1966 retiree earned an average return of 9.7%.
sentences.spoken: The portfolio of the nineteen sixty-six retiree earned an average return of nine point seven percent.

sentences.text: For the mirror retiree, the average is also 9.7%.
sentences.spoken: For the mirror retiree, the average is also nine point seven percent.

sentences.text: Not close.
sentences.spoken: Not close.

sentences.text: Identical.
sentences.spoken: Identical.

sentences.text: That is the geometric average, the compound rate that turns the starting dollar into the ending dollar.
sentences.spoken: That is the geometric average, the compound rate that turns the starting dollar into the ending dollar.

sentences.text: Multiplication does not care about order, so the same years in any order give the same average.
sentences.spoken: Multiplication does not care about order, so the same years in any order give the same average.

sentences.text: Even the simple arithmetic average, adding up the 30 returns and dividing by 30, is the same for both: 10.3%.
sentences.spoken: Even the simple arithmetic average, adding up the thirty returns and dividing by thirty, is the same for both: ten point three percent.

sentences.text: Same money in.
sentences.spoken: Same money in.

sentences.text: Same money out.
sentences.spoken: Same money out.

sentences.text: Same average.
sentences.spoken: Same average.

sentences.text: The only thing that differs is the order.
sentences.spoken: The only thing that differs is the order.

sentences.text: Watch the two balances year by year.
sentences.spoken: Watch the two balances year by year.

sentences.text: The question now: when does the order start to matter, and how much does it cost?
sentences.spoken: The question now: when does the order start to matter, and how much does it cost?

sentences.text: Year one.
sentences.spoken: Year one.

sentences.text: The 1966 retiree loses 4.8%.
sentences.spoken: The nineteen sixty-six retiree loses four point eight percent.

sentences.text: The mirror retiree gets the 1995 return first: a gain of 31.7%.
sentences.spoken: The mirror retiree gets the nineteen ninety-five return first: a gain of thirty-one point seven percent.

sentences.text: One year in, and the paths have already split.
sentences.spoken: One year in, and the paths have already split.

sentences.text: Then inflation starts to climb.
sentences.spoken: Then inflation starts to climb.

sentences.text: By 1969 it is 6.2% a year, and every withdrawal grows with it.
sentences.spoken: By nineteen sixty-nine it is six point two percent a year, and every withdrawal grows with it.

sentences.text: After inflation, stocks and bonds both lose money in 1973 and 1974.
sentences.spoken: After inflation, stocks and bonds both lose money in nineteen seventy-three and nineteen seventy-four.

sentences.text: In 1974 alone, the portfolio loses 14.7%, while prices rise 12.3%.
sentences.spoken: In nineteen seventy-four alone, the portfolio loses fourteen point seven percent, while prices rise twelve point three percent.

sentences.text: In 1966 dollars, the 1966 retiree ends 1974 with $461,000.
sentences.spoken: In nineteen sixty-six dollars, the nineteen sixty-six retiree ends nineteen seventy-four with four hundred sixty-one thousand dollars.

sentences.text: The mirror retiree, same year, same withdrawals: $1.27 million, also in 1966 dollars.
sentences.spoken: The mirror retiree, same year, same withdrawals: one point two seven million dollars, also in nineteen sixty-six dollars.

sentences.text: Here is why a bad start is so hard to undo.
sentences.spoken: Here is why a bad start is so hard to undo.

sentences.text: The withdrawal is still $40,000 in 1966 dollars, but it is now taken from a much smaller pile.
sentences.spoken: The withdrawal is still forty thousand dollars in nineteen sixty-six dollars, but it is now taken from a much smaller pile.

sentences.text: Every dollar withdrawn after a loss is a dollar that is not there when the recovery comes.
sentences.spoken: Every dollar withdrawn after a loss is a dollar that is not there when the recovery comes.

sentences.text: Analysts call this sequence-of-returns risk.
sentences.spoken: Analysts call this sequence-of-returns risk.

sentences.text: Good years do come.
sentences.spoken: Good years do come.

sentences.text: In 1975 the portfolio gains 23.6%, and in 1976 another 20.7%.
sentences.spoken: In nineteen seventy-five the portfolio gains twenty-three point six percent, and in nineteen seventy-six another twenty point seven percent.

sentences.text: But they compound on a balance that has already been cut, while the withdrawals keep rising.
sentences.spoken: But they compound on a balance that has already been cut, while the withdrawals keep rising.

sentences.text: Through the rest of the decade, inflation keeps rising.
sentences.spoken: Through the rest of the decade, inflation keeps rising.

sentences.text: In 1979 it reaches 13.3%.
sentences.spoken: In nineteen seventy-nine it reaches thirteen point three percent.

sentences.text: By 1981, the yearly withdrawal has grown to $108,553 in nominal dollars.
sentences.spoken: By nineteen eighty-one, the yearly withdrawal has grown to one hundred eight thousand five hundred fifty-three dollars in nominal dollars.

sentences.text: In 1966 dollars, it is still $40,000.
sentences.spoken: In nineteen sixty-six dollars, it is still forty thousand dollars.

sentences.text: Then, in 1982, the good years finally arrive.
sentences.spoken: Then, in nineteen eighty-two, the good years finally arrive.

sentences.text: That year the 1966 retiree gains 25.4%.
sentences.spoken: That year the nineteen sixty-six retiree gains twenty-five point four percent.

sentences.text: But the withdrawal now takes 16.9% of what is left.
sentences.spoken: But the withdrawal now takes sixteen point nine percent of what is left.

sentences.text: The boom comes too late.
sentences.spoken: The boom comes too late.

sentences.text: For the mirror retiree, those same years came first, when the balance was largest.
sentences.spoken: For the mirror retiree, those same years came first, when the balance was largest.

sentences.text: The gap widens every year.
sentences.spoken: The gap widens every year.

sentences.text: In 1986 it peaks.
sentences.spoken: In nineteen eighty-six it peaks.

sentences.text: In 1966 dollars, the mirror retiree is now ahead by $1.96 million.
sentences.spoken: In nineteen sixty-six dollars, the mirror retiree is now ahead by one point nine six million dollars.

sentences.text: At $40,000 a year in 1966 dollars, that gap would pay for 49 more years of withdrawals.
sentences.spoken: At forty thousand dollars a year in nineteen sixty-six dollars, that gap would pay for forty-nine more years of withdrawals.

sentences.text: From there, the story of the 1966 retiree is short.
sentences.spoken: From there, the story of the nineteen sixty-six retiree is short.

sentences.text: The mirror retiree meets the bad years late: the 1974 loss arrives in 1987, on a balance big enough to absorb it.
sentences.spoken: The mirror retiree meets the bad years late: the nineteen seventy-four loss arrives in nineteen eighty-seven, on a balance big enough to absorb it.

sentences.text: The account pays out its last $96,829, in nominal dollars, and hits zero in 1991.
sentences.spoken: The account pays out its last ninety-six thousand eight hundred twenty-nine dollars, in nominal dollars, and hits zero in nineteen ninety-one.

sentences.text: That last payment is short of the full withdrawal, and the final 4 years of the plan get nothing.
sentences.spoken: That last payment is short of the full withdrawal, and the final four years of the plan get nothing.

sentences.text: The mirror retiree finishes 1995 with $6.96 million in nominal dollars.
sentences.spoken: The mirror retiree finishes nineteen ninety-five with six point nine six million dollars in nominal dollars.

sentences.text: In 1966 dollars that is $1.44 million, more than the starting balance, after 30 years of withdrawals.
sentences.spoken: In nineteen sixty-six dollars that is one point four four million dollars, more than the starting balance, after thirty years of withdrawals.

sentences.text: Both portfolios averaged 9.7% a year.
sentences.spoken: Both portfolios averaged nine point seven percent a year.

sentences.text: The average did not decide who went broke.
sentences.spoken: The average did not decide who went broke.

sentences.text: So was 1966 a fluke?
sentences.spoken: So was nineteen sixty-six a fluke?

sentences.text: We ran the same rules for every start year from 1928 to 1996.
sentences.spoken: We ran the same rules for every start year from nineteen twenty-eight to nineteen ninety-six.

sentences.text: That is 69 retirements, each with 30 years of data.
sentences.spoken: That is sixty-nine retirements, each with thirty years of data.

sentences.text: The question for this part: what actually decides the outcome?
sentences.spoken: The question for this part: what actually decides the outcome?

sentences.text: Most of these retirees never ran out.
sentences.spoken: Most of these retirees never ran out.

sentences.text: In 65 of the 69 start years, the money lasted all 30 years.
sentences.spoken: In sixty-five of the sixty-nine start years, the money lasted all thirty years.

sentences.text: A retiree who started in 1982 under the same rules ended with $5.36 million in 1982 dollars.
sentences.spoken: A retiree who started in nineteen eighty-two under the same rules ended with five point three six million dollars in nineteen eighty-two dollars.

sentences.text: Even a retiree who started in 1929, the year of the crash, never ran out.
sentences.spoken: Even a retiree who started in nineteen twenty-nine, the year of the crash, never ran out.

sentences.text: Prices fell through the Depression, so the withdrawals shrank, and after inflation the first decade still averaged 3.9% a year.
sentences.spoken: Prices fell through the Depression, so the withdrawals shrank, and after inflation the first decade still averaged three point nine percent a year.

sentences.text: For many start years, the order of returns did no harm at all.
sentences.spoken: For many start years, the order of returns did no harm at all.

sentences.text: Surviving is not the same as thriving.
sentences.spoken: Surviving is not the same as thriving.

sentences.text: In 26 of the 69 start years, the retiree ended with less than the starting balance, after inflation.
sentences.spoken: In twenty-six of the sixty-nine start years, the retiree ended with less than the starting balance, after inflation.

sentences.text: 4 start years ran out of money, beginning with 1965 and 1966.
sentences.spoken: four start years ran out of money, beginning with nineteen sixty-five and nineteen sixty-six.

sentences.text: Then 1968 and 1969.
sentences.spoken: Then nineteen sixty-eight and nineteen sixty-nine.

sentences.text: Their long-run averages do not single them out.
sentences.spoken: Their long-run averages do not single them out.

sentences.text: After inflation, the 1966 retiree averaged 4.1% a year over all 30 years.
sentences.spoken: After inflation, the nineteen sixty-six retiree averaged four point one percent a year over all thirty years.

sentences.text: 17 start years had a lower real average than that, and never ran out.
sentences.spoken: seventeen start years had a lower real average than that, and never ran out.

sentences.text: After inflation, the 1969 retiree averaged 5.6% a year.
sentences.spoken: After inflation, the nineteen sixty-nine retiree averaged five point six percent a year.

sentences.text: The 1928 retiree averaged less: 4.9%.
sentences.spoken: The nineteen twenty-eight retiree averaged less: four point nine percent.

sentences.text: Yet 1928 ended with $1.21 million in 1928 dollars, and 1969 ran out of money in its 28th year.
sentences.spoken: Yet nineteen twenty-eight ended with one point two one million dollars in nineteen twenty-eight dollars, and nineteen sixty-nine ran out of money in its twenty-eighth year.

sentences.text: What the four failures share is their first decade.
sentences.spoken: What the four failures share is their first decade.

sentences.text: In every one of them, the portfolio lost money after inflation over its first 10 years.
sentences.spoken: In every one of them, the portfolio lost money after inflation over its first ten years.

sentences.text: After inflation, the first decade of the 1966 retiree averaged −1.8%.
sentences.spoken: After inflation, the first decade of the nineteen sixty-six retiree averaged minus one point eight percent.

sentences.text: In the first decade, the mirror retiree averaged 6.9% a year after inflation.
sentences.spoken: In the first decade, the mirror retiree averaged six point nine percent a year after inflation.

sentences.text: So, what decided it?
sentences.spoken: So, what decided it?

sentences.text: Not the average.
sentences.spoken: Not the average.

sentences.text: The first 10 years.
sentences.spoken: The first ten years.

sentences.text: To be precise: across all 69 start years, the 30-year real return still lines up best with how much is left at the end.
sentences.spoken: To be precise: across all sixty-nine start years, the thirty-year real return still lines up best with how much is left at the end.

sentences.text: But every retiree who ran out met a bad first decade.
sentences.spoken: But every retiree who ran out met a bad first decade.

sentences.text: The 9.7% average described the 1966 retiree perfectly, and it said nothing about 1991.
sentences.spoken: The nine point seven percent average described the nineteen sixty-six retiree perfectly, and it said nothing about nineteen ninety-one.

sentences.text: Now the limits of this analysis.
sentences.spoken: Now... the limits of this analysis.

sentences.text: This is history, not a forecast.
sentences.spoken: This is history, not a forecast.

sentences.text: It is US only, one country with one set of markets.
sentences.spoken: It is U.S. only, one country with one set of markets.

sentences.spoken: The sixty-nine windows overlap, so ninety-eight years of data hold only three separate thirty-year stretches.

sentences.text: And the model is bare: no taxes, no fees, one portfolio mix and one withdrawal rule.
sentences.spoken: And the model is bare: no taxes, no fees, one portfolio mix and one withdrawal rule.
